# Performance baseline (Q-14)

Measured 2026-10-12 from a cloud sandbox (egress via proxy) with `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`, Node v22.22.0. Raw data: `eval/perf/baseline-2026-10-12.json`. Raster endpoint: public titiler.xyz (default). Geo service configured: no.

Method: real tools via `executeTool`; global `fetch` wrapped from outside to log each request. **Cold** = in-process cache reset (`_resetCache`) then call; **warm** = immediate repeat in the same process (app's L1 cache populated). `titiler_npy` = the first concurrent batch of `/stac/feature.npy` reads (scene cloud scoring); `titiler_npy_after` = later `feature.npy` reads issued one after another (masked stats, then render data). Stage time is wall-clock union (parallel requests counted once); "no request in flight" is app compute or waiting between requests. Sandbox egress adds proxy latency to every request, so absolute numbers are pessimistic versus a server near the data; the stage proportions and request counts are what carry over. "Cold" is cold for the app only: titiler.xyz and the STAC APIs keep their own caches, so repeat runs of this script on the same AOIs and dates can be faster than a truly first visit (and the first-tile numbers especially).

## Where the time goes

All figures are medians over the 5 AOIs, cold, from the tables above (sandbox egress through a proxy; titiler.xyz public instance; STAC from Element84 earth-search). Timeline of one `fetch_ndvi` (Iowa, request offsets in ms): STAC search 0-723; six parallel `feature.npy` scoring reads (18.5 KB each) 723-1969; then three **sequential** `feature.npy` reads (74 KB, 40 KB, 474 KB) 1969-3016, 3030-3194, 3195-4219. Only 1% of the call is app compute; 99% is waiting on HTTP.

- **fetch_ndvi cold 4.66 s** = STAC 0.65 s (14%) + scoring batch 1.14 s (25%) + serial follow-up reads 2.61 s (59%). **render_raster 3.82 s** and **compute_spectral_index 3.20 s** have the same shape (21/33/46% and 12/23/65%). **fetch_dem 3.82 s** is a fully serial chain of 4 requests: opentopodata 0.63 s, then STAC 0.75 s, then SAS-sign 0.65 s, then a titiler tile probe 1.74 s (45% of the call).
- Tool cold times are 2.4-5.0 s and the app cache makes the exact repeat free: warm 0.03-0.07 s with 0 requests (fetch_dem warm still issues 1 request). The cache only helps identical repeats, not a new date, tool, or panned AOI.
- **Time to first tile is not the bottleneck; time to the tile URL is.** A z14 tile fetch measured 0.04-0.08 s here, but that run reused tiles titiler.xyz had already rendered in my earlier runs of the same script (the first, uncached-by-titiler run measured 0.06-0.95 s, median about 0.3 s, over the same AOIs; that JSON was overwritten). The `fetch_dem` layer's tile is slower (0.16-1.42 s; its 206 response on the probe took 1.7 s). Treat first-tile numbers as optimistic. The map cannot ask for a tile until the tool returns, which is 4.7 s for NDVI (about 1.8 s of it, STAC plus scoring, is spent before the scene is even chosen).
- **Budgets:** first pixels < 2 s: fetch_ndvi cold + tile is 4.71 s (2.4x budget, 2.7 s over), before adding the LLM planning round-trip that precedes it in the app (not measured here). AOI stats < 5 s: fetch_ndvi cold 4.66 s is inside the budget by only 0.34 s, and individual AOIs reached 5.0 s (and 5.3-6.2 s in earlier runs of this script); render_raster and compute_spectral_index are inside it. Style/threshold changes < 100 ms: not measured here.
- Run-to-run variance is large (same call, same AOI: compute_spectral_index 3.7 s then 2.4 s on Kasur in separate runs) because titiler.xyz is shared; read differences under about 1 s with caution.

### The 3 biggest concrete wins this implies

1. **Run the follow-up reads concurrently and start them earlier (about 2.6 s, 56-65% of cold time, is serial).** After the scoring batch, the stats read, the render read and the third read go one after another (parallelism x1.0: 74 KB 1.0 s, 40 KB 0.2 s, 474 KB 1.0 s). They depend on the chosen scene, not on each other, so issuing them together bounds the tail by the slowest (about 1.0 s) instead of the sum; the data supports saving up to roughly 1.0-1.5 s per call. This is also where Q-15 (emit the layer as soon as the scene is chosen, stats afterwards) takes effect.
2. **Drop or shrink the scene-scoring batch (1.1 s, 25%, 6 requests).** Each scoring read is only 18.5 KB, so these are latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound; six requests still cost 0.8-1.2 s of wall time (individual reads 0.4-1.9 s). The STAC response (about 126 KB) already carries scene-wide cloud cover, which the tool summary quotes. Scoring on STAC metadata plus a single read, or a server-side composite (Q-18), removes most of this and moves the tile URL to roughly 0.7 s after the call starts. Together with win 1 this is the path from about 4.7 s to the 2 s first-pixels budget.
3. **Cut per-request latency to the raster server (titiler.xyz: 135 requests, median 760 ms, p90 1.2 s, 99 s of summed request time, 10.5 MB total).** Requests of 18-470 KB all take 0.4-1.9 s, so each request is dominated by fixed latency (connection, COG header reads, shared public instance) rather than transfer size. This is the Q-17 item (own TiTiler in AWS us-west-2 next to the `sentinel-cogs` data, with the GDAL settings in the queue); Q-17's done-when is this table re-run. Part of this latency is the sandbox proxy, so the absolute gain is unproven until re-measured from a deployment next to the data.

Also visible but outside the top 3: `fetch_dem` spends 1.74 s (45%) in a blocking tile probe and runs its STAC lookup and SAS signing strictly after the elevation call (Q-15 already plans to drop `verifyTileUrl`; the DEM request and the imagery lookup are independent and could overlap).

### Reference: geo service

`services/geo` (the Python composite service, used only when `GEO_SERVICE_URL` is set) was measured separately by another agent at 11.5 s cold / about 1.2 s warm for a September NDVI composite over Kasur. That is a different product (multi-scene cloud-masked composite) and environment, so it is not comparable with the single-scene rows above; it is included only as a reference row.

## After Q-15 (concurrent follow-up reads, no tile probe, early layer)

Re-run on 2026-10-12 with `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 npx tsx scripts/perf/baseline.mts --label=after-q15` (same 5 AOIs, same sandbox proxy, public titiler.xyz). Full tables: `eval/perf/after-q15-2026-10-12.md`, raw data `eval/perf/after-q15-2026-10-12.json`. The baseline above is unchanged. Variance between runs is large (shared titiler.xyz), so differences under about 1 s are weak evidence; this is one run per cell. The proxy adds latency to every request; absolute numbers are pessimistic.

What changed: the SCL-512 and band-512 reads run together; the statistics read for the candidate starts when its reflectance gate starts (the gate is still the arbiter of which scene wins, Q-60 unchanged); `fetch_ndvi` and `compute_spectral_index` draw a provisional layer once the gate passes; `verifyTileUrl` is gone.

| tool | median cold, before | median cold, after | median time to first drawable layer, after |
|---|---|---|---|
| fetch_ndvi | 4.66 s | 3.81 s | 3.64 s |
| compute_spectral_index | 3.20 s | 2.60 s | 2.16 s |
| render_raster | 3.82 s | 2.91 s | 2.91 s (no preview: its stretch needs the statistics) |
| fetch_dem | 3.82 s | not measured | not measured |

- **fetch_dem was not re-measured.** `api.opentopodata.org` returned HTTP 522 (origin down) throughout the re-run, so every call timed out at 15 s with the standard "could not reach the elevation API" failure (a connectivity failure, correctly reported, not an absence of data). The change (no 1.74 s probe; STAC lookup and SAS signing overlapping the elevation call) is covered by unit tests only. Expected effect from the baseline timeline: the probe (45%) disappears and 1.3 s of imagery lookup moves under the 0.6 s elevation call, but this is not measured.
- Warm (app cache) is unchanged: 0.04-0.1 s, 0 requests.
- Request counts are unchanged (9-10 per call); the saving comes from overlap, not fewer reads. `titiler_npy_after` parallelism went from x1.0 to x2.3-2.4.

### Time to first layer event through the HTTP route (fetch_ndvi, stub LLM)

`node scripts/perf/first-layer.mjs --aoi=kasur,lahore,beauce --runs=2` against the production standalone server (PORT=3160, AGENT_ALLOW_STUB=1, NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1). Seconds from request start; no model round-trip is included (the real app adds one planning round-trip before any tool starts, not measured here).

| AOI | cold: first layer (provisional) | cold: final layer / done | warm: first layer |
|---|---|---|---|
| lahore | 2.47 s | 3.14 s | 0.12 s |
| beauce | 2.63 s | 2.94 s | 0.05 s |
| kasur | 4.88 s (no earlier preview: the gate rejected or the scan went past the first batch, so preview and final coincide) | 4.88 s | 0.10 s |

Against the **< 2 s first-pixels budget: not met cold** (2.5-4.9 s here; warm 0.05-0.12 s meets it). The preview now arrives 0.3-0.7 s before the final layer on AOIs where the first scene passes the gate, and the whole call is about 0.8 s shorter, but the path to the first pixel is still STAC search (0.2-1.1 s) + six SCL scoring reads (1.5-2.4 s wall, latency-bound) + the plausibility gate. Going under 2 s needs that chain removed, not overlapped further: a server-side composite (Q-18) or a raster server next to the data (Q-17), or scoring on STAC metadata plus one read. Part of these numbers is sandbox proxy latency; from a server near the `sentinel-cogs` bucket the same chain would be shorter, unproven until Q-17 is measured.

Stage timings are now emitted live: `tool_call` completed carries `timings` (stac_search, scene_scoring, stats, render, first_layer, llm_plan, total, in ms; stages overlap so they do not sum to total) and `geoagent_stage_duration_seconds{tool,stage}` is on `/api/metrics`.
